extracted.intended_audience: readers of early-19th-century travel journals, historians of exploration, and general educated public interested in African geography and natural history
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from an early-19th-century travel narrative (including appendices) covering African geography, natural history (botany), commerce statistics, and practical expedition procedures. Contains descriptive argumentation about river-identification hypotheses, practical how-to instructions, and logistical notes for overland travel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments supporting the hypothesis that the Congo is the Niger
rubrics_metrics.description: In support of the hypothesis which identifies the Congo with the Niger, the following arguments may be alleged: 1. The great magnitude of the Congo. 2. The probability that this river is derived from very remote sources, perhaps considerably north of the equator. 3. The fact, that there exists a great river north of the equator, (the Niger,) of which the termination is unknown, and which may, perhaps, form the principal branch of the Congo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as the only substantive grounds on which the supposition can fairly rest; etymological conjectures, supposed resemblances of names, or African narratives alone are treated as too arbitrary or fanciful unless supported by collateral proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal objections against the Congo–Niger identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal objections are: 1. It supposes the Niger to lie through the vast chain of the Kong Mountains, making it difficult to understand how the Niger could penetrate that barrier. 2. The estimated course (if same as Congo) would be considerably more than 4000 miles, an improbably large length compared with known great rivers. 3. Lack of traces of Mahometan doctrines or institutions on the coasts where the Niger is supposed to terminate, which one might expect if the Niger flowed through regions with Mahometan influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These objections are described as weighty and formidable; length and mountain-penetration arguments are emphasized as serious physical improbabilities, and absence of cultural/Islamic influence on the coast is used as circumstantial evidence against the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for assessing 'magnitude' of a river
rubrics_metrics.description: The magnitude of a river depends much less upon the length of its course than upon the number of auxiliary streams which fall into it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative comparison: the Ganges is very large because of many auxiliary streams, while the Nile's course is longer but comparatively less in magnitude. Rivers not fed by auxiliary streams may even become smaller in consequence of great length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors affecting formation of river deltas
rubrics_metrics.description: The formation of deltas depends on circumstances such as the depth of the sea at the mouth of the rivers and perhaps other not fully understood factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples noted: some great rivers (Amazon, Plata, Oronoko, now Congo) lack prominent deltas; difference appears due in part to depth of sea at the river mouth. Thus one should not universally assume great rivers form deltas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of evidence vs. native testimony in geographical conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Etymological conjectures, resemblances of names, affinity of languages, and native travellers' narratives are classed as too arbitrary and fanciful and generally unreliable unless supported by collateral proof from other less exceptionable sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor repeatedly emphasizes preference for positive/physical evidence (soundings, reports of magnitude, observations) over linguistic or purely narrative African evidence when assessing large-scale geographical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of the 'Fang Jani' (self-burning tree) reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Specimens called 'Fang Jani' appeared as branches of a Pandanus species with black and withered shoots and bases that looked like charcoal, but on examination the black was due to a disease (a parasitic fungus, probably of the nature of Puccinia), not actual burning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although many natives assert seeing spontaneous fires, the botanical examination failed to support true combustion; the editor notes that few natives had actually seen it burning, and botanical/experimental analysis should be preferred to uncorroborated local belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and reporting standard for botanical specimens (e.g., 'Kino')
rubrics_metrics.description: Specimen of 'Kino' received from Mr. Park proved to be a species of Pterocarpus not yet described by any botanical writer; origin of known drugs should be traced to plant species when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where only partial specimens are sent (e.g., 'Tribo' root only), identification and assessment are limited; small sample sizes prevent decisive experiments. Scientific naming and reference to existing literature (or noting novelty) are the appropriate responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical procedures for organizing loads and animals on an expedition
rubrics_metrics.description: Mode of marching and packing: asses and loads were marked and numbered with red paint; a number of each allotted to each of the six messes, further subdivided so every man could tell at a glance which ass and load were his; asses also numbered with large figures to prevent theft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organization included assigning persons to front/centre/rear (Mr. George Scott and others front, Lieutenant Martyn centre, Mr. Anderson and author rear), hiring additional asses when necessary, and reducing baggage if insufficient transport. Practical measures (marking, numbering) to prevent theft and confusion are emphasised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local superstition and campsite precaution (Bentang tree example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Slatee warned that sleeping under a particular Bentang tree would cause death; on inspection spear-heads, bone-ashes and a half-burnt rope were found in the tree root notch, prompting the party to remove bundles and sleep elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The account implies an expeditionary standard: heed local intelligence and visible ritual signs; move camp when local chiefs advise danger or show ritual artifacts indicating past violence—pragmatic respect for local knowledge and caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etiquette and negotiation practices with local chiefs (Slatees)
rubrics_metrics.description: When paying respects to Slatees (district masters), gifts of liquor or rum were customary; demands for greater gifts could be expected (example: a Slatee at Samee initially demanded ten jugs but accepted two after negotiation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expedition practice included offering presents (rum, kegs) to curry favour or secure safe passage; anticipate negotiation and occasional exactions by local rulers, budget and plan accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical recipe/process: dyeing cotton blue with indigo leaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Process described: collect large quantity of wood-ashes (mimosa nitta or mimosa pulverulenta preferred), make a strong lye ('sai-gee') by pouring water through the ashes into an unglazed earthen vessel with a hole and straw; fill a pot a quarter full with indigo leaves and add sai-gee to half fill, stir once or twice daily for four days; then fill pot nearly full of sai-gee and stir frequently four more days until it ferments and throws up a copper-coloured scum; let it rest one day; on the tenth day put the cloth in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific timing (ten days total), choice of woods for ashes, use of unglazed vessel with hole and straw, and fermentation observation (copper scum) are given as practical markers for readiness. Quantity and handling affect results; procedure is stepwise and time-sensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting African commerce statistics post-abolition
rubrics_metrics.description: Imports and exports between Great Britain and Africa showed a large increase in the years following abolition of the slave trade (e.g., imports from Africa 1808 £374,306; 1809 £383,926; 1810 £535,577; exports 1808 £820,194; 1809 £976,872; 1810 £693,911).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor (and an experienced African Company officer) offers interpretations: differences between export and import values might be explained by enemy capture of goods, contraband used by slave traders, or accounting for gold dust and bills of exchange. Caution is urged when reading official returns (loss of custom-house books) and when accounting for disguised or contraband trade.
